questions.subject: FRENCH
questions.topic: The aller family and its members
questions.learningObjective: name the member of the aller family in use and say what it adds
questions.stem: A colleague writes « Je vais vérifier le tableau des horaires » and then goes and checks it. What is the member of the aller family doing, and what does it add?

options.text: aller plus an infinitive, so the line announces a plan rather than a finished act
s'en aller, so the claim is that the writer has already left the building
options.misconception: reads the sentence as a report that the departure is complete

options.text: y aller, so the sentence reports that the writer is on the platform at this moment
options.misconception: hears a stated destination and concludes the writer is under way

options.text: a plain aller of motion, so the writer is crossing the room as she speaks
options.misconception: takes a near-future use of the verb as a description of movement now

questions.explanation: Aller carries more than one job, and the infinitive after it is the signal of the near-future reading, where the sentence puts an intention in front of the listener rather than a fact. 'Je vais vérifier' is therefore a plan, and the writer is free to change her mind, which is exactly what the following action shows. The trap is that a present-tense sentence about movement is common in French, so 'Je vais' invites a reading of somebody already on her way; a speaker who takes that reading misses that the clause is about what will happen, not about where the writer is standing.
questions.hint: Ask whether the speaker could still change her mind after saying this.

questions.subject: FRENCH
questions.topic: The mettre family and its members
questions.learningObjective: read remettre as a member of the mettre family and name the sense it adds
questions.stem: A notice on a board reads « La réunion est remise à jeudi soir ». Which member of the mettre family carries the sentence, and what sense does it add?

options.text: remettre, which here means to put a date back, so the meeting is postponed
mettre, which means the meeting was handed over to the room on Thursday
options.misconception: keeps the plain verb and reads the notice as a delivery report

options.text: admettre, which means the notice is accepting a proposal that starts on Thursday
options.misconception: reaches for the prefix ad- because the notice is a form of agreement

options.text: se mettre, which means the meeting has started by itself on Thursday evening
options.misconception: attaches the reflexive pronoun to the verb without checking the sense

questions.explanation: The prefix re- on remettre gives the family a second job, and in a notice about a date it means the opposite of fixing: the meeting has been moved rather than held. Recognising that the same root does two things is the whole point of learning a family, because a learner who knows only 'to put' will either misread this notice or avoid the word altogether. The distractor that sounds closest is mettre, since the noun and the verb genuinely do share a root in the sense of handing something over; what is missing is the idea of a second date, and without it the notice says nothing about postponement.
questions.hint: Ask what the word says about the original date of the meeting.

questions.subject: FRENCH
questions.topic: The prendre family and its members
questions.learningObjective: recognise an idiom built on prendre and say what it claims
questions.stem: After you admit a hard week, a friend answers « Je te prends au sérieux ». Which member of the prendre family does the phrase use, and what does it tell you?

options.text: prendre au serieux, which treats the words as true and worth acting on
prendre pour, which reads your words as a joke you meant from the start
options.misconception: sees the fixed expression and assigns it the sense of the pour phrase

options.text: comprendre, which reports that the two of you now share one view of the week
options.misconception: hears a shared root and assumes the phrase means mutual agreement

options.text: prendre de, which asks the listener to fetch something you have just named
options.misconception: reads the phrase as a request because the verb is one of taking

questions.explanation: Prendre enters into a set of fixed expressions that are not built on the image of holding at all, and « prendre au sérieux » claims something about the truth of what was said rather than about the listener's conduct. That is why a speaker chooses it to close a conversation: it answers the admission with weight. The neighbouring phrases make the point better than any list would. 'Prendre pour' introduces a mistaken judgement, and 'comprendre' names agreement between two minds, so a learner who treats the shared root as the meaning will pick either of them and lose the reassurance entirely.
questions.hint: Ask what the friend is saying about the words rather than about himself.

questions.subject: FRENCH
questions.topic: The faire family and its members
questions.learningObjective: read a faire idiom as a whole and say what it concedes
questions.stem: A colleague accepts a weekend invitation with 'Je ne me ferai pas prier'. What does the expression add to a plain yes?

options.text: the speaker accepts readily, as though no persuasion were needed at all
the speaker will accept only after several refusals and a long argument
options.misconception: reads se faire prier literally, as if the speaker had to be begged

options.text: the speaker declines the invitation politely and expects no reply
options.misconception: confuses the idiom with a formula of polite refusal in letters

options.text: the speaker will ask to skip the greeting at the door on arrival
options.misconception: invents a second meaning for faire that no speaker attaches to it

questions.explanation: Faire builds a long family of expressions whose members are learned as phrases rather than as words, and « ne pas se faire prier » is one of the most frequent. The negative is what carries the sense: the speaker describes what will not happen, namely being asked twice, and a listener reads the sentence as a cheerful yes with an edge of impatience. A learner who translates the pieces in order gets the opposite, because prier means to beg and the reflex se faire suggests something done to the speaker, so the phrase looks like a complaint. Native usage keeps the whole thing in view and takes the word prier as the part that never actually occurs.
questions.hint: Ask what the speaker says will not be done to them.

questions.subject: FRENCH
questions.topic: Currently as a false friend
questions.learningObjective: reject the English sense of a word that looks shared
questions.stem: A news bulletin says « Le prix est actuellement de quatre euros » about a museum ticket. What does the adverb mean in that line?

options.text: at this moment, as opposed to what the price will be at some later point
in fact and in reality, as opposed to what some people have claimed
options.misconception: carries the English sense of actually into a sentence about a price

options.text: in the long run, as opposed to what happens on a single day of sales
options.misconception: reads a time adverb as covering a trend rather than an instant

options.text: roughly the same as, as opposed to what the ticket used to cost
options.misconception: treats the adverb as a comparison when it marks only a moment

questions.explanation: Currently exists in French and does mean 'right now', and the word actually is one of the most tempting imports a learner makes, because the two share most of their letters and the contexts of price and fact both invite the stronger English word. What makes the false friend dangerous is that the English sense is not wrong in general; it is simply not what this word does. A price that is 'currently' four euros is a figure with an expiry date, and the sentence exists to warn the listener that the figure will move, which is a different job from correcting a rumour. Learning the pair together is more useful than learning either alone, because the two languages will otherwise keep borrowing each other's habits.
questions.hint: Ask whether the sentence warns about a moment or about a rumour.

questions.subject: FRENCH
questions.topic: Bookshop as a false friend
questions.learningObjective: say what a learner has asked for when the words only partly match
questions.stem: A traveller in Paris wants to buy a novel and asks « Où est la librairie la plus proche ? » What has the traveller asked for?

options.text: a shop that sells books, which is a different sort of place from a library
a building where books may be read on the spot and borrowed without payment
options.misconception: reads the -erie ending as though it named a place for reading

options.text: a shop that deals only in second-hand books and in printed pictures
options.misconception: adds a restriction to the word that the French does not contain

options.text: an office that keeps the official written records of the town
options.misconception: borrows the English sense of a records office and drops books

questions.explanation: French keeps two words that English merges into one: librairie is the shop where books are sold, and bibliotheque is the place where they are kept. A traveller who asks for the librairie has asked for a shop, and will be directed to a street of shops rather than to a reading room, which is a real and expensive mistake in a city where the two can be half an hour apart. The word is not a cognate at all, so there is nothing in its shape to hold on to, and the ending that looks like an English -library is a French -erie with a very wide family of its own. Learning the pair as a pair is the cheapest way to keep them apart.
questions.hint: Ask whether the traveller intends to walk out carrying the book.

questions.subject: FRENCH
questions.topic: Sensible as a cognate that drifts
questions.learningObjective: tell apart a shared spelling that carries two different senses
questions.stem: A colleague praises a draft with « Ton texte est très sensible, il touche juste ». What is the praise about?

options.text: the draft's sensitivity to tone and detail, not its display of good judgement
the draft's practical good sense, in the way an advisor talks about money
options.misconception: keeps the English sense, which is where a shared word most often misleads

options.text: the draft's sensitivity to cold weather while the pages were being written
options.misconception: fixes on the physical sense the English word shares in another context

options.text: the draft's plainness, since a sensitive text in French avoids strong opinions
options.misconception: invents a new sense instead of choosing between two that already exist

questions.explanation: This is a cognate that has not drifted so much as forked: French uses sensible in the sense of responsiveness, and 'il touche juste' confirms it, since hitting the right note is a matter of feeling the right register. The English word kept the older sense of showing judgement, so a speaker of English arrives with praise already loaded and hears a compliment about common sense. Nothing about the spelling could have prevented that, which is the point worth taking away: a shared form is evidence about history and not about meaning. A useful habit is to ask what the sentence would be about in English, because here the answer, a sensitivity to something, settles the choice in a second.
questions.hint: Ask what the second clause, about hitting the right note, is evidence of.

questions.subject: FRENCH
questions.topic: Assister as a false friend
questions.learningObjective: reject an imported sense and name what the French verb reports
questions.stem: A union newsletter says « Elle assistait aux réunions tous les mardis » about a staff delegate. What is the verb reporting?

options.text: that she was present at the meetings, whether or not she ever spoke
that she lived close to the meeting room, which made attendance easy for her
options.misconception: keeps the English sense of residing in a place, which has a French word

options.text: that the meetings paid her to prepare the room before the others arrived
options.misconception: turns presence at a meeting into paid preparation work

options.text: that she listened through a closed door rather than join the group inside
options.misconception: borrows a partiality that the preposition aux does not express

questions.explanation: Assister means to attend or to be present, and the preposition is what says in what capacity: assister à une réunion is being there, while assister quelqu'un means to help somebody. The sentence is a report of presence and nothing more, which is why a delegate's attendance can be recorded from it without any question of what she said. English keeps the older sense of living at a place, and a learner who imports it produces a sentence that points at housing rather than at a calendar. The two false friends so far, librairie and assister, share a feature worth noticing: the imported sense is not a rare old meaning but the commonest one in English, which is exactly why it feels like the translation.
questions.hint: Ask what the preposition a is doing after the verb.

questions.subject: FRENCH
questions.topic: Brutal as a cognate whose sense moved
questions.learningObjective: explain a drift from an older sense to a present one
questions.stem: A chef writes « Le risque est brutal : la cuisson dure douze minutes exactement. » What is the adjective describing?

options.text: the process, which is sudden and unadorned rather than cruel
the cook, whose manner has been harsh towards the staff all morning
options.misconception: reaches for the English sense of cruel and then finds no cook to attach it to

options.text: the result, which the writer treats as savage and unhuman
options.misconception: keeps the cruel sense but attaches it to the dish instead of the verb

options.text: the taste, which the diner finds excessively strong and unpleasant
options.misconception: makes the adjective a complaint about flavour rather than about timing

questions.explanation: Brutal in French describes something raw, abrupt and without ceremony, and a cooking process of exactly twelve minutes fits that reading exactly: there is no margin in it. English kept the older, more violent sense and also grew a slang one in which the word means strikingly good, so the three senses sit side by side there and none of them is the French one. This is the clearest case of drift in the set, because the word has not simply narrowed or widened; it has moved to a different part of the metaphorical field. A learner who hears the English meaning in a French kitchen will look for cruelty in a sentence that only ever claims precision.
questions.hint: Ask what the twelve minutes are being described as, rather than who is doing them.

questions.subject: FRENCH
questions.topic: Liberal as a cognate whose sense moved
questions.learningObjective: read a political label in an older non-political sense
questions.stem: A historian reads a 1902 report: « Le jury s'est montré libéral et a accordé des notes très hautes. » What does the adjective mean there?

options.text: generous and open-minded in what it allowed, not left-leaning in politics
left-leaning in politics, which is the sense an English reader expects first
options.misconception: applies the modern political sense to a report written before the party existed

options.text: free of any charge for the sitting, since the word describes what a fee was
options.misconception: turns a judgement about conduct into a statement about money

options.text: untrained in the subject, since an open jury was one appointed by chance
options.misconception: invents a third sense instead of choosing between two that are real

questions.explanation: Liberal describes generosity and openness about what one allows, and a jury described that way has given marks far above its habit, which is what the second half of the sentence reports. The political sense is genuinely older in English than the generous one, so this drift runs in the opposite direction to brutal: the word left the field of conduct and arrived in the field of parties. A dated document is the right place to see this clearly, because a reader who supplies a 1902 committee with a modern alignment will read an argument into a page that is only describing generosity. Register and date are doing real work here, not decoration.
questions.hint: Ask what the second half of the sentence says the jury did.

questions.subject: FRENCH
questions.topic: Titles and the formal register
questions.learningObjective: say what a full title sets about the relationship in writing
questions.stem: A notice on a laboratory wall reads « Docteur Morel, salle 3 » and never « Doc Morel ». What has the full title set?

options.text: a professional register, in which a title is kept alongside the surname
an invitation to the reader to use the first name from the first line
options.misconception: reads a formal title as though it signalled warmth and ease

options.text: a claim that this is the only doctor working in the whole building
options.misconception: reads a room number as though it settled a question of rank

options.text: a legal instruction, in which the surname must be written in capitals
options.misconception: conflates a courtesy form with a rule of official writing

questions.explanation: The surname in a notice does not stand alone; it hangs from a title that says what the person is to the institution, and keeping the two together is the ordinary mark of a professional register in writing. Dropping the title while keeping the name produces a different, warmer line, which is why « Doc Morel » changes the temperature of the notice even though the words are the same. What the title does not do is claim anything about the person being the only one of the kind, and it certainly is not a legal requirement, since nothing about capital letters is involved. The value of noticing this in a notice is that it is the most common written French a learner ever meets, and the title is a fixed slot rather than a phrase to be improvised.
questions.hint: Ask what the title contributes that the surname does not.

questions.subject: FRENCH
questions.topic: Informal address in a working message
questions.learningObjective: identify the informal markers in a message to a known person
questions.stem: A message to a work friend opens « Salut Léa, ça te dit samedi ? » Which contrast with a formal note is being made?

options.text: the two markers leave the register open among people who already know each other
the two markers make the message binding in the way a signed contract would be
options.misconception: treats a casual greeting as though it created a legal obligation

options.text: the two markers withdraw the offer unless a reply arrives within a single day
options.misconception: reads an informal proposal as though it set a deadline

options.text: the two markers place the writer higher in rank than the person addressed
options.misconception: assumes that informality always signals seniority in a workplace

questions.explanation: Salut and ca te dit both belong to the spoken register that people use with people they know, and putting them in writing tells the reader immediately that no distance is being claimed. That is a genuine choice, not a lack of politeness: the message goes to a colleague the writer already knows, and the alternative would be a note about an arrangement nobody has to be stiff about. The trap is to read informality as either a legal instrument or an insult, neither of which the markers carry. What they do carry is a claim about footing, and the claim can be checked: if the same two words opened a message to a client or a judge, they would read as careless rather than friendly.
questions.hint: Ask what the two words promise about the relationship before the content begins.

questions.subject: FRENCH
questions.topic: The cue that decides between the two pronouns
questions.learningObjective: name the social cue that settles a choice of pronoun
questions.stem: A shop assistant says Madame and uses vous to a customer in her sixties, while a classmate of the same age is addressed as tu. What decides the two?

options.text: the setting and the relationship: service and age pull toward vous, familiarity toward tu
the grammar: vous is not allowed to follow a title such as Madame in one address
options.misconception: believes a rule about titles and pronouns that the language does not have

options.text: the region: one pronoun is used north of the Loire and the other only in the south
options.misconception: confuses vocabulary that varies by region with a choice of pronoun

options.text: the hour of the day: tu belongs to a morning greeting and vous to an evening one
options.misconception: invents a time rule out of two greetings that do exist for different reasons

questions.explanation: French has one familiar pronoun and one polite one, and what separates them is the footing of the exchange rather than anything in the sentence. At the counter, the assistant is paid to serve and the customer has not asked to be treated as a friend, so vous follows, and it would follow whatever the customer's age. In a classroom the two are peers, and peers use tu. Both the age and the length of acquaintance enter as evidence, but neither settles it, which is why an older customer is still addressed formally and a close friend of twenty is not. The most reliable version of the rule is therefore about the setting, with the pronouns as the visible result.
questions.hint: Ask what each exchange is doing before anyone speaks.

questions.subject: FRENCH
questions.topic: Keeping the polite distance
questions.learningObjective: explain what a refusal of the familiar pronoun does to a relationship
questions.stem: A retired colleague offers « On se tutoie ? » and a new manager answers « Non, je préfère que nous nous vouvoyions » about the same friendship. What is being done?

options.text: keeping the polite distance, since workplace rank can override an old friendship
accepting the proposal twice, once as colleague and once as private friend
options.misconception: hears agreement in a sentence whose plain sense is a refusal

options.text: rejecting the new manager's own post, since a pronoun is a sign of lower rank
options.misconception: turns a choice of address into a statement about the job itself

options.text: asking to meet outside working hours before any pronoun has been settled
options.misconception: reads a social decision as a proposal about the calendar

questions.explanation: A refusal of tu is a normal and often welcome move, and what it signals is that the person on one side is keeping a distinction they will need later, most often because of an office they hold. The manager is not rejecting the friendship so much as declining to conduct it in a register that would make the job harder to manage; the pronouns are how the distance gets said out loud, once, so nobody has to keep guessing. What the sentence does not do is change anybody's position or make a proposal about the weekend, and a reader who expects some larger consequence has read a small courteous act as a dramatic one. The formula nous nous vouvoyions is the formal way of setting it.
questions.hint: Ask why a person would want the distinction to be visible to both speakers.

questions.subject: FRENCH
questions.topic: Two words for a long-distance coach
questions.learningObjective: read a regional split in everyday vocabulary
questions.stem: Two regional timetables list the same coach service to the same towns. What word are they most likely to print?

options.text: le car in the west and le bus in the north, for one vehicle and one set of routes
le car in both places, since the word has been standard on timetables for a century
options.misconception: assumes a single national term because the routes and vehicles are the same

options.text: le bus in both places, since le car is only used for a vehicle towing a trailer
options.misconception: invents a technical restriction on le car to remove the regional split

options.text: le tram in both places, since a regional timetable never lists a road vehicle
options.misconception: replaces the question of naming with a claim about what timetables contain

questions.explanation: The same vehicle is called le car in much of the west and le bus in the north, and both are ordinary rather than old, so a learner who hears one of them in a timetable and expects it everywhere will be understood anyway. Regional vocabulary differs from dialect in an important respect: it is a matter of which standard word a town has settled on, not of anything strange being said. That is why these pairs are worth learning as pairs, since guessing the wrong one costs nothing in a conversation but does cost something at a ticket counter. The two words are also easy to remember once the map is known, since the split roughly follows the old northern city and the rural west.
questions.hint: Ask which name a north-western passenger would expect on the printed line.

questions.topic: Two names for the town hall
questions.learningObjective: hold a regional pair of terms apart in each direction
questions.stem: An address in Angers and an address in Aix-en-Provence each name the town hall. Which pair is the usual regional split?

options.text: la mairie in the west and l'hotel de ville in the south
la mairie in the south and l'hotel de ville in the west
options.misconception: has the two regions the right way round and so names the wrong building

options.text: l'hotel de ville in both places, since la mairie is only used in small villages
options.misconception: shrinks la mairie to villages when both words name the same building

options.text: la mairie in both places, since l'hotel de ville names the office of the prefect
options.misconception: gives l'hotel de ville a different function, which the pair does not have

questions.explanation: La mairie is the usual word in the west and the north, and l'hotel de ville is the usual one in the south, and both are perfectly standard where they are not the local habit. Nothing about the building differs: the same office keeps the registers and issues the same papers, and a letter addressed to either in the wrong region still arrives. That is the useful thing to know about regional pairs, because the fear of sounding odd is usually what stops people using them, and the cost is nil. Learning them with the map attached, west and north for one, south for the other, is far more reliable than trying to absorb both words as interchangeable synonyms.
questions.hint: Ask which word a reader in Aix would expect on the envelope.

questions.subject: FRENCH
questions.topic: The article with a bread term
questions.learningObjective: read a regional habit in the article as a variation, not a change
questions.stem: A shopper in Rouen asks « Vous me vendrez du pain ? » and one in Marseille the same question with de la baguette. What differs?

options.text: only the local habit with the article on a bread term, and not the meaning at all
the shape of the loaf, since the two phrases name different products by law
options.misconception: turns a difference in wording into a difference in what is sold

options.text: the price, since a bread term always asks for the loaf to be weighed
options.misconception: links the article to a sale practice that the words do not mention

options.text: the politeness, since one of the two articles asks the seller to hurry
options.misconception: reads a grammatical habit as though it carried a social signal

questions.explanation: The two questions ask for the same thing, and both are said by people who are understood perfectly well. Some regions use the partitive with a bread word where others use de la, and neither choice changes the meaning, the quantity or the price. This is worth separating from the regional vocabulary of the last item: here the words are the same and only the article in front of them has moved, which is a smaller and safer thing to learn. The trap is to treat a variation as evidence of a difference, so that a person concludes the shopkeeper in Marseille is selling some other product. A useful check is simply to ask what the sentence would mean, and in both cases the answer is the same loaf.
questions.hint: Ask what the shopper wants in each of the two questions.

questions.topic: Three local names for a small drink
questions.learningObjective: hold three regional terms for one thing without merging them
questions.stem: At a zinc in Lille, in Lyon and in Marseille someone orders « un petit » of beer. What does the phrase name in each place?

half a glass in one town and a third in another, with a whole one in the third
options.misconception: turns three names for one drink into three different measures

options.text: a glass that comes free with the first course, since petit describes a bonus
options.misconception: reads a size word as though it settled what the customer pays

options.text: a full glass, since the adjective describes the head of foam and not the drink
options.misconception: attaches the word to the wrong part of what is served in the glass

Regional vocabulary is reassuring rather than troublesome once it is understood as variation: the bar is selling the same quantity of beer, and the person behind it is not going to correct a customer who guessed the word.
questions.hint: Ask what quantity of beer is being ordered at each counter.

questions.subject: FRENCH
questions.topic: A fixed closing formula in a formal letter
questions.learningObjective: recognise a formula that is learnt whole rather than composed
questions.stem: A letter ends « Je vous prie d'agréer, Madame, l'expression de mes salutations distinguées. » What has the writer done?

options.text: used a fixed closing formula and taken the recipient's rank for granted
asked for a favour that the recipient is expected to grant on the spot
options.misconception: reads the verb prier as a request rather than as part of a formula

options.text: warned that the letter will arrive later than the reader had expected
options.misconception: gives the closing formula a content that belongs to a letter body

options.text: withdrawn an earlier request out of politeness at the last possible moment
options.misconception: assumes a conventional ending cancels what the letter has already asked

questions.explanation: The sentence is a formula, and formulas are the part of a language a learner stores whole rather than builds word by word, because a speaker does not compose them any more than they compose a greeting. What the formula does is mark the end of the letter, take the reader's title at face value, and hand over the last word in the most deferential shape available. The trap is to read prier as a request, which is quite reasonable and quite wrong here: nobody is asking for anything at this point in the letter, and a person who treats the closing as a favour will be puzzled by the answer. Storing three or four such formulas whole is worth more than understanding every word in them.
questions.hint: Ask whether anything is still being asked for at the end of the letter.

questions.stem: A line at a service window reads « Votre dossier est incomplet. Merci de revenir demain. » Which formula is still required?

options.text: s'il vous plait, because the sentence asks the reader to act rather than to note
no formula at all, because a factual notice never needs a politeness marker
options.misconception: decides from the tone of the notice rather than from what it asks for

options.text: excusez-moi, because the writer is asking to be forgiven for the delay
options.misconception: supplies a formula of apology for a fact the writer did not cause

options.text: bien a vous, because a sign-off is the only politeness a notice can carry
options.misconception: puts a letter formula where a request for an action stands

questions.explanation: The second sentence of the notice is an instruction, not a piece of news, and instructions addressed to a stranger carry a courtesy marker whether or not the writer feels like adding one. Merci is already there, and it does real work in the notice, but it follows the request rather than softening it, so the softening still has to come from s'il vous plait. This is the practical content of politeness in a language with two pronouns: it is not a mood of the writer but a marker attached to particular speech acts, of which asking somebody to come back is one. A learner who attaches markers to moods will add them to condolences and forget them at a counter, which is where they are needed.
questions.hint: Ask whether the reader is being told something or being asked to do something.

questions.stem: A delivery slip prints « M. Ravel, 4 rue des Lilas » in a list of addresses. What has the reader been given?

the initial of a first name, so Ravel is the surname and the letter is separate
options.misconception: reads the mark as a first-name initial, which a surname-hung title never is

options.text: the word Maitre, a courtesy used in France only toward lawyers and notaries
options.misconception: borrows a French title from another legal setting and attaches it to any name

options.text: the abbreviation of modele, which marks a printed form attached to the slip
options.misconception: invents an office form reading where the line is a personal address

questions.explanation: The mark is a courtesy title, Monsieur, cut to its initial and hung in front of the surname, which is where French expects it. options.text: nomenclature, so the entry names the official list the address belongs to

the dish built around the main ingredient, and so served after the starter

questions.learningObjective: name a literary period from the concern its writers shared

questions.stem: Stage one: say which pronoun an assistant should use with a customer she has served for years, and give the cue that decides it. Stage two: rewrite her greeting as it would sound with tu.

answer.exemplar: Stage one: vous, because the setting decides it rather than the length of acquaintance. She is paid to serve, the customer has not proposed anything else, and ten years of custom does not turn a service relation into a friendship, however friendly the two have become. Stage two: « Bonjour Madame, je vous cherche un billet pour Lyon » becomes « Salut, je te cherche un billet pour Lyon », and the pronoun carries the whole change of footing with it, from a clerk addressing a customer to one person speaking to another. The trap is to let the years do the deciding, because « elle est cliente depuis dix ans » sounds like evidence to a reader of English, where familiarity is what selects the familiar form; in French the counter is a different room from the friendship.

questions.explanation: The two stages test the same thing from opposite ends, because a rule that cannot change a sentence is not yet a rule. The first stage is a question of footing: a paid service relationship keeps the polite pronoun however warm the exchange has become, and the cue is what the two are doing rather than how long the shop has known the customer. The second stage is a check on that answer, because writing the greeting with tu forces a decision about the salutation as well, and the greeting will not stay formal with a familiar pronoun in front of it. Items like this earn their place because the second half catches the first half being remembered too loosely.
questions.hint: Ask what the two people are doing, not how long they have known each other.

a street, a town and the date on which the parcel is promised to arrive

questions.stem: A library card reads: « Hugo, Victor (1802-1885). Les Misérables. Paris, 1862. » A student says this entry is a fact about a book rather than a review of it. What can a reader check on it?

the author's own ranking of the book among his other novels and their sales
options.misconception: expects a card to carry a judgement, which is the work of a review and not of a record

options.text: a summary of the plot together with the number of copies printed in 1862
options.misconception: reads a factual record as though it carried both an argument and a print run

options.text: the prize that the book won and the name of the publisher who issued it
options.misconception: supplies two fields a catalogue would print if it held them, which it does not

The wrong answers each add something the card does not carry. A plot summary belongs in a different record altogether, and sales figures or a prize would have to be printed on the card for a reader to check them, which they are not. The author and the year are the two fields a citation actually needs.

questions.topic: Locating the topic sentence in a paragraph
questions.learningObjective: pick the sentence that controls the rest of a paragraph
questions.stem: A paragraph reads: « La ville s'est agrandie en quinze ans. Les constructions ont suivi. Les anciens habitants ont été déplacés. C'est ce dernier point qui fait débat aujourd'hui. » Which sentence is the topic sentence?

the second, which names the one fact that every other sentence has to support
options.misconception: picks the sentence in the middle because it links the other two, not because it covers them

options.text: the third, because a paragraph is best opened by its most concrete detail
options.misconception: mistakes the most concrete sentence for the one the others are gathered under

options.text: the fourth, since the debate named there is what the paragraph is finally for
options.misconception: picks the sentence that promotes a fact to an argument and calls it the opening

The third is the most concrete detail and therefore the most tempting, since detail is easy to notice; but detail is what a topic sentence collects rather than what it is. Stage two: say which sentence would have to change if the paragraph were about housing costs instead.

Stage two: the fourth sentence would have to change, because « C'est ce dernier point qui fait débat aujourd'hui » marks displacement as the live question, while a paragraph about housing costs would mark the rise in cost as the live question. questions.explanation: The two stages are set together because a controlling idea and a topic sentence are easy to confuse, and the second stage is what separates them. In this paragraph the two happen to be the same sentence, so the paragraph cannot teach the difference; changing the subject does. A paragraph about housing costs would keep its opening and its second sentence, keep the third as a fact, and change only the sentence that promotes a fact to an argument. A student who can do that has stopped reading paragraphs as a list of true sentences and started reading them as a claim with support, which is the whole subject in a single move.

questions.topic: Learning a family as phrases rather than words
questions.learningObjective: set out a method that makes a family recoverable and apply it
questions.stem: A learner must learn the family built on prendre without memorising a list. Describe a method that makes the members recoverable, and apply it to two members you name.

answer.exemplar: Build the family as a set of slots rather than as a list of words, and put a meaning in each slot. « Prendre le train » is a slot for travelling, « prendre un rendez-vous » for arranging a meeting, « prendre froid » for a change of state, and « ne pas s'en prendre à quelqu'un » for blame; what the learner stores is not a stem ending in -re but a verb with the thing it governs and the job it does. Learning two of these as slots makes the rest of the family reachable, because a new member slots into a place the learner already has, and the two named here sit at the two ends of the range, motion at one and blame at the other. The method fails if the endings are memorised, since the endings are exactly the part that never predicts the meaning.

questions.explanation: A list of a family is the least useful form of learning it, because the items arrive with no relation to each other and nothing for a new item to hang on. Phrases are better, since each one carries a whole use, and slots are better again, because they carry a category that several members can share. The test of any such method is what happens to the next member the learner meets: with slots, the question is which place it belongs in, and with a list there is no question at all. The two examples above show the range the family spans, from travelling to being blamed, which is wide enough that a learner who knows only the literal sense of taking will be surprised by at least half of it.
questions.hint: Ask what a new member of the family has in common with the ones already known.

warning that a single large task is beyond the reach of any workshop forever

questions.topic: What a concluding sentence has to do
questions.learningObjective: diagnose a weak concluding sentence and replace it
questions.stem: A student's paragraph on the cost of heating ends « En conclusion, j'ai parlé du chauffage. » Explain what that sentence fails to do, and supply a concluding sentence that would work.

A concluding sentence draws the claim the paragraph has built to its sharpest form and leaves the reader holding the claim rather than a list. « Le chauffage représente donc le premier poste du budget d'un ménage, bien avant l'électricité » names the claim, keeps the vocabulary of the paragraph, and hands over one thing to remember. A conclusion that names the topic has done the work of the opening a second time, and the paragraph ends without ever saying what it argued. The test is whether a reader who has not seen the paragraph would learn anything from the last sentence alone, and the student's sentence fails it while the replacement passes. The added stress on the claim is what makes the replacement a conclusion rather than a fifth example, and the connector is doing the work of tying the claim back to the evidence that was given.

questions.topic: What a connector commits the writer to
questions.learningObjective: say what a concessive connector claims about two facts
questions.stem: A writer joins two sentences: « Le train a eu du retard. Cependant, les voyageurs sont tous arrivés avant l'heure de correspondance. » What does the connector claim?

options.text: it grants the first fact and then sets the second against it in spite of it
it withdraws the first fact, since the second makes it pointless to report anyway
options.misconception: treats a concessive link as though it deleted what came before the turn

options.text: it makes the second fact the cause of the first, in the order of cause and effect
options.misconception: reads a link of consequence where the surprise in the facts shows there is none

options.text: it links the two facts in time, with the first happening before the second
options.misconception: confuses the order in which the sentences are printed with the relation they assert

The four choices cover the relations a connector can assert, and substituting any of the others would change what the writer is arguing. Students who treat connectors as joining words rather than as claims produce sentences that are grammatical and mean nothing at all.

questions.subject: FRENCH
questions.topic: Why one connector cannot be swapped for another
questions.learningObjective: explain what three different connectors claim about one pair of facts
questions.stem: Three students join the same pair of facts with « mais », « cependant » and « donc », and a reader hears three different arguments. Explain what each connector commits the writer to.

answer.exemplar: The connector is the writer's claim about the relation, so changing it changes the argument. « Il pleut, mais je sors » refuses the weather as a reason and goes out anyway: the first fact is conceded and then overridden. « Il pleut, cependant je sors » does the same work in a written register, conceding the fact and then standing against it. « Il pleut, donc je sors » makes the first fact the reason for the second and overrides nothing at all. The trap is to treat the three as decorative links between the same two clauses; a reader who hears them as interchangeable hears no argument, and an editor who swaps them has silently changed what the writer claimed.

questions.explanation: The reason a connector deserves study in a composition unit is that it is the only place where the writer's stance towards the facts can live, since the two clauses are otherwise identical. That is why the three versions carry three different claims rather than three styles of one claim, and why only two of them are concessions. The written and the spoken forms of a concession differ in register rather than in meaning, which is the useful part of the mais and cependant pair, and the third shows what an altogether different relation sounds like. A learner who cannot say which relation a connector asserts will not be able to choose one under pressure.
questions.hint: Ask which of the three lets the first fact stand.

questions.topic: Turning an untestable claim into a testable one
questions.learningObjective: restate an untestable cultural claim and say what to look for
questions.stem: A travel sheet says « the French are a private people who never discuss money in public ». Restate the claim so a reader could check it, and say what you would look for.

answer.exemplar: A claim a reader can check names who, where, what and how often, and the sentence on the sheet supplies only a generalisation and the word « never », which cannot be observed at all. A checkable version reads: « In France, people tend to talk less about what things cost than people in the United States do, so a shopkeeper may give a price without apologising for it. » Now it can be looked for: whether the price is said aloud at the counter, whether a discount is mentioned unprompted, how a café bill is passed across a table. The trap is the strengthened modal, since a word like never makes a statement unfalsifiable and therefore says nothing at all.

questions.explanation: Generalisations about a national character are the commonest untestable writing in any language, and the defect is not the prejudice so much as the grammar of the claim, which admits of no observation. Restating it means giving it a shape something could be counted against: a place, a behaviour, and a tendency rather than a certainty. That is a demanding move for a learner, because the restated claim is weaker and therefore feels like a loss, when in fact it is the only version anybody could check. The reward is that a checked claim can be reported back to somebody, and the original one can only be repeated.
questions.hint: Ask which word in the sentence makes it impossible to observe.

questions.subject: FRENCH
questions.topic: The moves that make a paragraph work
questions.learningObjective: order the moves of a paragraph from claim to restatement
questions.stem: Four moves from one paragraph have been printed out of order. Which sequence produces a paragraph that argues rather than merely states?

options.text: The controlling idea, stated as a claim the writer is prepared to defend
The evidence, given as two or three concrete cases that support the claim
The counter-consideration, named and answered so the reader holds the objection too
The restatement, which hands the claim back in its sharpest available form

questions.explanation: A paragraph that argues puts the claim in first, so the reader knows what the evidence is for, and it puts the objection before the close, so that the close is not merely a repetition. The four moves in this order leave the writer having done three things: stated a claim, supported it, and dealt with the strongest thing against it, which is what makes the last sentence a conclusion rather than an echo. The moves can appear in other orders in real paragraphs, and a claim sometimes arrives last, but the sequence given here is the one a writer builds deliberately when the argument is not yet familiar to the reader.
questions.hint: Ask which move the reader needs before the evidence can be understood.

questions.subject: FRENCH
questions.topic: The parts of a formal letter in order
questions.learningObjective: order the parts of a formal letter as they are actually written
questions.stem: Four parts of a reply to an official letter have been printed out of order. Which sequence is the one a French formal letter actually uses?

options.text: The opening, which gives the sender's name and the reason for writing at all
The reference, which names the earlier message or the file this letter answers
The request, stated as one clear sentence the reader is able to act upon
The closing, which thanks the reader and leaves a formal sign-off in place

questions.explanation: A French formal letter moves from who is writing and why, to what earlier document it is answering, to what the reader is being asked to do, and only then to the closing. The order is not decorative: the reference has to come before the request because the reader needs to know which matter the request concerns, and the request has to come before the closing because the closing is what lets the letter end. The last move is where register is decided, since a formal sign-off after a plainly worded request is what makes the whole letter read as official rather than as friendly.
questions.hint: Ask which part the reader needs in order to know what is being asked of them.

questions.subject: FRENCH
questions.topic: Choosing a closing and then writing it
questions.learningObjective: choose a closing by its register, then write one that holds it
questions.stem: A letter to an official you have never met ends « Je vous prie d'agréer, Madame la Directrice, l'expression de mes salutations distinguées. » Stage one: say why that closing fits and what would disqualify a friendly one. Stage two: write the sentence you would send, keeping the rank you are acknowledging.

answer.exemplar: Stage one: it fits because the two have never met and the reader holds an office the writer does not, so the closing has to carry the distance rather than assume a contact. What disqualifies a friendly one is not warmth in itself but the presumption behind it, since « Salut, à bientôt » tells a stranger that the writer expects to see them again, and nobody has said that. Stage two: « Je vous prie d'agréer, Madame la Directrice, l'expression de mes salutations distinguées. » A stock of these formulas is what a writer reaches for, and the choice is governed by the two cues rather than by taste: the stranger and the office. A letter that gets the register wrong at the close loses whatever the body of it achieved.

questions.explanation: The closing is where a register decision becomes visible to a reader, and it is decided by two facts about the relationship rather than by the writer's mood. That is why the same writer can justify a formal close one day and an affectionate one the next, and why a learner should not choose a closing by which one sounds nicer. The two stages check each other: naming the cue and then writing the sentence is what turns a rule about register into something usable at the keyboard. The test afterwards is simple, since if the reader could answer with a short neutral line and neither party would be embarrassed, the closing was right.
questions.hint: Ask what a reader who has never met the writer would expect in the last line.
